Here are verse-by-verse notes on Job 26, drawn from the available commentaries.

---

## Job 26: Notes for a Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### v. 1 — "Then Job answered:"

This begins Job's long final discourse (chs. 26–31), which silences his three friends entirely. The pronouns in vv. 2–4 are singular, suggesting Job addresses Bildad specifically (the last speaker, ch. 25), though the sarcasm is aimed at all three. Job's tone is sharp and biting — remarkable for a man in his condition.

- **URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-26/
- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-26.html (Gill)

### vv. 2–3 — "How you have helped the powerless… How you have counseled the unwise and provided fully sound insight!"

These verses are heavy with sarcastic irony. Job mocks Bildad: "What a wonderful helper you've been to one who is powerless! What magnificent counsel you've given to one without wisdom!" The point is that Bildad has offered no real help, comfort, or practical wisdom — only recycled platitudes. Matthew Henry notes that Bildad ought to have brought consolations rather than terrors; Christ knows how to speak what is proper for the weary (Isa 50:4), and his ministers should not grieve those whom God would not have made sad. Gill suggests the statements could be understood as Job saying: if the controversy needed talk of God's majesty, he himself could say far greater things.

### v. 4 — "To whom have you uttered these words? And whose spirit spoke through you?"

Job questions both the audience and the source of Bildad's words. JFB (Jamieson, Fausset & Brown) comments: "For whose instruction were thy words meant? If for me, I know the subject (God's omnipotence) better than my instructor." The question "whose spirit came from you?" is a jab: the spirit behind Bildad's speech was not God's (contrast Job 32:8), but a borrowed sentiment from Eliphaz (Job 4:17–19; 15:14–16). Ellicott reads it differently — "Was it not my own breath, my own teaching, that came forth from you?", meaning Bildad was only repeating what Job himself had already said. The NIV rendering, "Whose spirit spoke from your mouth?", captures the penetrating nature of the question.

### v. 5 — "The dead tremble — those beneath the waters and those who dwell in them."

The Hebrew word translated "the dead" is *Rephaim*, a term used for the shades or departed spirits in the underworld. The Pulpit Commentary describes them as "the ghostly, bloodless forms" leading a joyless, shadowy existence, akin to Homer's depiction in the *Odyssey*. The Hebrew verb rendered "tremble" (some translate "are formed" or "are pierced") suggests either writhing in pain or trembling in terror before God. JFB says the point is that God's power reaches even to the realm of the dead — not only to "high places" (heaven) as Bildad said in 25:2. Constable notes that the *Rephaim* in Ugaritic culture were the elite dead, thought to be the most powerful departed; Job declares that even these tremble under God's authority. Gill also discusses the possibility that "those inhabiting the waters" could refer to sea creatures, coral, or even the spirits of those who perished in the flood.

### v. 6 — "Sheol is naked before God, and Abaddon has no covering."

Sheol (the realm of the dead) and Abaddon ("Destruction," a poetic synonym for the place of the lost; cf. Rev 9:11) are completely exposed to God's sight. Nothing in the underworld is hidden from Him. The Pulpit Commentary connects this to Hebrews 4:13 — all things are "naked and opened unto the eyes of Him with whom we have to do." Gill observes that the grave, though a "land of darkness" to us, is fully visible to God, who preserves the dust of the dead for the resurrection. This verse grounds Job's larger point: God's dominion extends to every realm — heaven, earth, and under the earth.

### v. 7 — "He stretches out the north over empty space; He hangs the earth upon nothing."

This is widely regarded as a remarkable anticipation of modern astronomy. Ellicott states plainly: "If these words mean what they seem to do — and it is hard to see how they can mean anything else — then they furnish a very remarkable instance of anticipation of the discoveries of science." The Pulpit Commentary says this idea was "scarcely reached by astronomers in general, at any rate till the time of Hipparchus." In contrast to ancient myths that the earth rested on elephants, turtles, or Atlas's shoulders, Job declares it hangs on nothing — suspended in space by God's will alone. Gill notes that some Jewish writers interpreted "nothing" as the earth's centre of gravity, but the plain sense is that God's power alone sustains it. Constable concludes: "Job viewed the earth as sustained only by God."

### v. 8 — "He wraps up the waters in His clouds, yet the clouds do not burst under their own weight."

God binds vast quantities of water inside clouds — an image of waters stored in heavenly "water-skins" — yet the clouds do not tear open and release a deluge (cf. Gen 7:11; 8:2). Ellicott says this "apparent defiance of what we know as the laws of gravitation" displays God's mastery. The Pulpit Commentary notes that God retains the rain until He wills to release it. James Smith (Precept Austin) writes: "How often have we seen those great water-carriers rolling along the heavens… 'Great and marvelous are Your works, O Lord.'"

### v. 9 — "He covers the face of the full moon, spreading over it His cloud."

The Hebrew is debated. Some translations (like the BSB footnote) read "He covers the face of His throne." The Pulpit Commentary supports this: "God veils the outer side of his heavenly throne, the side turned towards earth, by drawing the clouds between." Ellicott similarly reads, "He covereth the face of his throne in the heavens, spreading his rack of cloud upon it." JFB says, "God makes the clouds a veil to screen the glory not only of His person, but even of the exterior of His throne, from profane eyes." Gill agrees: God's throne is invisible behind clouds and darkness (Psalm 18:11). The alternative "full moon" reading sees God's cloud passing over the moon's bright face as another display of His sovereignty.

### v. 10 — "He has inscribed a horizon on the face of the waters at the boundary between light and darkness."

God has drawn a circular boundary — the horizon — where sea and sky appear to meet, marking the limit between day and night. The Pulpit Commentary explains the ancient cosmology: the earth is surrounded by water (the ocean stream), and above is the circle of the hemisphere where sun and stars run; within is light, outside is darkness. Ellicott describes this as the perfect circle of the sea-horizon, "which is the limit apparently of light, and beyond which is darkness." Constable says the circle "is the horizon that appears as a boundary for the sun." Gill notes that the bounds are as permanent as the cycle of day and night will last, tied to God's covenant promise after the flood (Gen 8:22).

### v. 11 — "The foundations of heaven quake, astounded at His rebuke."

"The pillars of heaven" (KJV) or "foundations of heaven" are poetic imagery for the great mountains that seem to bear up the sky. The Pulpit Commentary says the earthquake is represented as caused by the mountains' terror at God's rebuke (cf. Psalm 29; 104:7; Nahum 1:4; Revelation 6:12–14). JFB identifies God's "rebuke" with thunder reverberating from cliff to cliff (Hab 3:10; Nahum 1:5). The imagery is personification: even the most stable parts of creation tremble when God speaks. Matthew Henry sees this as part of the displays of God's almighty power in the heavens above.

### v. 12 — "By His power He stirred the sea; by His understanding He shattered Rahab."

"Rahab" (meaning "proud one" or "arrogance") is here not Egypt (as in Isaiah 51:9 and Psalm 87:4), but a mythical sea monster symbolising chaotic forces opposed to God. Ellicott notes that if Rahab were taken as Egypt, it could only refer to the Exodus, which some would use to date the book. However, Constable states plainly: "Rahab was a mythical sea monster that was symbolic of evil (cf. Job 9:13)." The Pulpit Commentary describes Rahab as "some huge monster of legendary fame." The first clause — "He stirred the sea" — can be read as either stirring up or stilling; Ellicott prefers calming, fitting the context of God's mastery over nature. David Guzik (Enduring Word) makes the important point that Job is taking ancient mythological language about cosmic battles (e.g., Marduk vs. Tiamat, Baal vs. Yam) and making the Lord God the sole hero — a deliberate monotheistic polemic against pagan pantheons. James Smith sees Rahab as representing pride and arrogance: "By His understanding is human pride smitten through."

### v. 13 — "By His breath the skies were cleared; His hand pierced the fleeing serpent."

The "fleeing serpent" (Hebrew *nachash*) is a parallel to Rahab — another chaos monster. The Pulpit Commentary suggests this may allude to the mythical dragon thought to swallow the sun or moon during eclipses; the ceremony of beating off the dragon with cries and noises was practiced among the Turks and others. Ellicott says the expression "the crooked serpent" (KJV) most likely refers to the forked lightning-flash, "though it is difficult to determine whether any, or what mythological ideas may underlie the expression." Others take it as the constellation of the Northern Dragon. Constable calls the fleeing serpent "a synonym for Rahab." David Guzik ties this to Satan, noting that Satan is often represented as a dragon or serpent (Genesis 3; Revelation 12–13), and the sea as a threatening place in the Jewish mind. The ancient rabbinic mythologies held that an evil serpent resisted creation, and God killed it to bring order. Guzik again stresses that Job de-personalised the pagan deities: "Job depersonalized Yam by using the definite article (the sea), thus expressing his innate monotheistic theology."

### v. 14 — "Indeed, these are but the fringes of His ways; how faint is the whisper we hear of Him! Who then can understand the thunder of His power?"

All that Job has just described — the underworld, the cosmos, the clouds, the horizon, the quaking mountains, the subdued sea, the pierced serpent — these are merely the "edges" or "outskirts" of God's ways (Hebrew *qetsot*, "extreme boundaries"). The Pulpit Commentary renders it: "Lo, these are ends of his ways — but the outlines or sketches — the nearest and most familiar evidences of his government of the world; and what a gently whispering word it is that we hear! — but the thunder of his omnipotence who can understand?" JFB contrasts the "whisper" with the "thunder" — the partial revelation now against the full disclosure of God's power (cf. 1 Corinthians 13:9–10, 12). Ellicott says: "We can only hear the faintest whisper of His glory, and cannot understand or endure the full-toned thunder of His majesty." Matthew Henry notes that while creation reveals God's power, redemption eclipses all other wonderful works: through redemption "we may draw near, and taste his grace, learn to love him, and walk with delight in his ways."

This verse also makes a key theological point about Job's position: Job demonstrates that he knows more about God's greatness than his friends do, yet even this is only a whisper. His suffering remains unexplained by the "exact retribution" theory of his friends; he cannot understand and they cannot explain, but he rests in his own faith (Ellicott).

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

On the whole of Job 26, the major Protestant traditions surveyed are largely in agreement on the meaning of this chapter. The chapter is so centred on God's power in creation that it does not touch on the distinct doctrinal disputes (e.g., predestination, perseverance, spiritual gifts, sacraments) that typically divide traditions. However, some differences in emphasis do appear:

**Baptist (Gill, Garner-Howes):** Gill (a Reformed Baptist) treats the "dead" in v. 5 as possibly including the pre-flood giants and even discusses the resurrection of those buried at sea, tying the passage to Revelation 20:13. He reads the cosmos scientifically, discussing magnetism, gravity, and the earth's centre. Matthew Henry (Presbyterian/Puritan) takes a more devotional approach, emphasizing that Job's friends failed to consider original sin and God's purifying designs in affliction.

**Reformed (JFB, Constable, Pulpit):** JFB and Constable both stress that vv. 5–14 are a carefully structured tour through God's domains — hell (vv. 5–6), earth (v. 7), sky (vv. 8–11), sea (v. 12), heavens (v. 13) — showing God's comprehensive sovereignty. The Pulpit Commentary uniquely draws parallels to classical literature (Homer, Lucretius, Ovid) and Persian/Arab poetry.

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik):** Guzik emphasizes the spiritual-warfare reading of vv. 12–13. He sees Rahab and the fleeing serpent as manifestations of Satan, and the sea as a symbol of chaos and threat that God subdues. This approach makes a stronger connection to Genesis 3, Revelation 12–13, and the cosmic battle motif than other traditions. Guzik also stresses the "practical help" emphasis in vv. 1–4 — friends so focused on being right that they forgot to help the sufferer.

**Anglican (Ellicott):** Ellicott is characteristically measured on the mythological language, noting the difficulty of determining what mythological ideas underlie "the crooked serpent," while leaving open both a natural reading (lightning) and an astronomical one (constellation). He treats Job 26:14 as "Job's final reply to the arguments of his friends" — Job is more conscious of God's grandeur than they are, but this does not explain his suffering; he rests in faith without explanation.

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship:** Constable (drawing on Andersen and L'Heureux) provides the most detailed modern scholarly notes. He identifies the *Rephaim* (v. 5) with the elite dead of Ugaritic culture and notes that Job's language deliberately subverts Canaanite mythology. Scholars also note a textual-critical debate: some have argued vv. 5–14 are actually Bildad's or Zophar's words, misplaced. However, Constable reports that the content is more consistent with Job's theology than the friends', and the lack of any textual reference to a different speaker makes this view "unattractive."

- **URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-26.html (Constable)

**Catholic and Orthodox readings:** No results were returned from the searches of newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org. The search budget was exhausted before these could be specifically retrieved.

**Modern popular teachings (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace):** No results from the approved sites addressed Job 26 through these lenses. The chapter's focus on God's transcendent power and human limitation in suffering does not naturally lend itself to prosperity-oriented interpretations, and none were found in the sources searched.
